hooks.text: A postage stamp that declared Pluto unexploded inspired a spacecraft to visit it.
Why did a postage stamp taunt scientists into building a Pluto probe?
One postage stamp carried all the way to Pluto sparked an entire mission.

title: The Stamp That Sent a Probe to Pluto
description: How a defiant United States postage stamp inspired NASA's New Horizons mission to fly past Pluto.

beats.text: A postage stamp declaring Pluto unexploded inspired a spacecraft to visit it.
beats.visual: USPS Pluto Not Yet Explored stamp, 1991

beats.text: In nineteen ninety-one, the postal service released a set showing every planet alongside its visitor except the ninth.
beats.visual: 1991 planetary exploration postage stamp set by USPS

beats.text: Pluto's stamp simply read, Pluto: Not Yet Explored.
queries: Pluto Not Yet Explored stamp close up

beats.text: The phrase irked researchers so much that it became a call to arms for a new mission.
beats.visual: Principal Investigator Alan Stern working on mission plans, 2005

beats.text: On January nineteen, two thousand six, New Horizons launched as the fastest object ever sent from Earth.
beats.visual: Launch of the New Horizons spacecraft on an Atlas V rocket, 2006

beats.text: A Jupiter gravity assist shaved three years off the voyage, sending the probe speeding toward the solar system.
beats.visual: Jupiter as photographed by the New Horizons spacecraft, 2007

beats.text: On July fourteen, twenty fifteen, the spacecraft finally completed its historic close flyby of Pluto.
beats.visual: High-resolution color view of Pluto's surface captured by New Horizons, 2015

beats.text: Hidden onboard all along was that exact nineteen ninety-one stamp, delivered right to its destination.
beats.visual: Artist concept illustration of the New Horizons spacecraft in flight, 2015
